name: Elena Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, and thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential and your name won't be on it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm not sure I'll be much use, mind. I don't have anything to do with computers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's no problem at all. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hughes and Son, a small family builder in our town, mostly extensions, garages and the odd barn conversion for people out in the villages. There's Mr Hughes, his son Rhys, Kieran and me, and I'm the junior, so I mix, fetch, strip out old kitchens and do the first-fix carpentry when Rhys lets me. I'm not great with measuring, I measure twice and still cut wrong sometimes, and Mr Hughes just says 'that's the lesson, love' and takes it out of nobody's pay. I love it when a family moves into a room we built and makes it theirs. What wears me out is the mud in winter, every site in the villages is a bog by November.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what I'd expect, to be honest. It's all on phones, isn't it, not on building sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I thought as much. People in town would agree, I think, most of them don't trust any of it. I'm not on the internet much, so I'd say it at chapel or at the pub with Owen, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can get on with my life. Owen and I are getting married next September at the chapel, and we've got a deposit saved for a house on the edge of town. If nothing changes, I keep working for Mr Hughes and learning, and that's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different at all. I'd keep working, keep saving with Owen, and carry on planning the wedding with my mum. We've got enough put by for the deposit and a good bit over, because I've lived at home and we've both been careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people in town don't trust it. Why do you think that is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've had a lot of things promised that never helped us. The bank shut, the bus goes twice a day now, and every new thing seems to be for people in cities. So when someone says AI will change everything, people round here just think, change it for who?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything at Hughes and Son changed because of technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys uses a laser level now, and he does his quotes on a laptop instead of in the notebook. Mr Hughes still does his in the notebook, in pencil. I'm more like Mr Hughes. I don't even have the internet on my phone most of the time.

S0.say: I'd say I thought as much, and most people in town would agree. I'd say it at chapel or the pub with Owen rather than online.
S0.think: It means I can get on with my life: marry Owen next September and buy a house on the edge of town. If nothing changes I keep working for Mr Hughes and learning, and that's all I want.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving with Owen exactly as now. Carries on planning the wedding with her mum, with enough saved for the deposit and some over from living at home.
S0.quote: When someone says AI will change everything, people round here just think, change it for who?
S0.fieldNote: Elena's life is rooted in her small town, chapel and family, and her plans are concrete: a wedding and a house. Her distrust of AI is tied to a wider feeling that new things are made for cities. She avoids technology entirely, even more than her boss's son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs changing. I suppose that's already happening, in the big places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be slower round here, it always is. I'd say people should learn a proper trade, because there'll always be a need for someone who can build a wall. I'd say it to my younger cousins especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a bit worried about firms like ours. There's already a company that sells factory-built garden rooms and extensions, dropped on by crane in a day, and they've taken two jobs off Mr Hughes this year. If that spreads, small builders like us get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Mr Hughes and wait to see what happens. I wouldn't go on any computer course, that's not me. If Rhys started using some new gadget, I'd let him get on with it and do the parts that still need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A little knot in my stomach about Mr Hughes, more than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Mr Hughes more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's sixty-one, and the firm's his whole life, his father started it. If work dries up, I could go and labour for someone else, there's plenty of building round here. But he'd lose the thing his family built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger cousins about this, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get an apprenticeship and learn to do something properly with your hands. Don't sit in a bedroom on a computer waiting for some job that doesn't exist. That's what I'd tell them, anyway, whether it's right or not.

S1.say: I'd say it'll be slower round here, as it always is. People should learn a proper trade, because there'll always be a need for someone who can build a wall.
S1.think: I'm worried about small firms like ours, because a factory-built extension company has already taken two jobs off Mr Hughes this year. If that spreads, we get squeezed.
S1.do: Keeps working for her boss and waits to see what happens, refusing any computer course. Lets her boss's son handle new gadgets and sticks to the parts that still need hands.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in her stomach more for her boss than for herself.
S1.quote: If work dries up, I could go and labour for someone else, there's plenty of building round here.
S1.fieldNote: She already sees one concrete threat: factory-built extensions undercutting her small firm. Her worry is for her boss and the family business more than herself. She believes firmly in apprenticeships and hands-on trades, and admits she might be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years? That's before the wedding's paid off, near enough. I don't like that one at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and someone should stop it. Big companies in other countries deciding that nobody here gets to work. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other, because I wouldn't trust the government to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be finished as a builder before I'd properly started. And Owen's family farm, if robots can do that too, I don't know what happens to them. It's the house I'd lie awake about, signing for a mortgage just when it all comes down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd not buy the house. We'd still get married, but small, at the chapel with tea in the hall after, not the big do at the hotel. We'd move into the cottage on Owen's family farm, which is empty, and keep every penny of the deposit as savings. And I'd lean on my family and the chapel, because that's what they're there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Scared, really. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the deposit as savings. How long would that keep you going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we lived in the cottage with no rent, a few years, I'd think. I've not done the sums properly. Owen's better at that than me, he does the farm books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't trust the government. If it offered an income to everyone who lost work, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd want to work for what I've got, like my dad did. But if it was that or Owen's family going under, I suppose I'd swallow my pride. I wouldn't like it, though.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and someone should stop big companies in other countries deciding nobody here gets to work. Families and churches will have to look after each other, because I wouldn't trust the government to.
S2.think: I'd be finished as a builder before I'd properly started, and I don't know what happens to Owen's family farm. It's signing for a mortgage just as it all comes down that I'd lie awake about.
S2.do: Drops the house purchase and scales the wedding down to the chapel with tea in the hall. Moves into the empty cottage on Owen's family farm, keeps the deposit as savings and leans on family and the chapel.
S2.feel: Alarmed and scared, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: We'd still get married, but small, at the chapel with tea in the hall after, not the big do at the hotel.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits her life plans more than her job: the house, the wedding, Owen's farm. She turns to family and faith first and would take public money only as a last resort, reluctantly. She hasn't worked out how long the savings last and relies on Owen for the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of breathing space, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's keep our heads and look after our own. I'd say the young ones should still learn trades, because people will want a person they know doing their house for a while yet. I'd say it at chapel, at home, at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd think it's still too soon. I'd get my few years of being a proper builder, but I'd be watching all the time. And I'd worry about having children into it, which we want to do after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, nothing fancy but not tiny either. We'd hold off on buying the house for a couple of years and live in the farm cottage meanwhile, saving harder. I'd keep working for Mr Hughes for as long as he's got work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every day, but I could still sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will want a person they know doing their house for a while yet. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, round here. People ring Mr Hughes because they knew his father. Mrs Price on the hill had us back three times because Rhys fixed her gate for free once. I don't think a robot gets asked in for tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Owen decide about children, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pray on it, and talk to our parents. My mum had me at twenty-five with nothing, and they managed. I think we'd still have them, maybe a bit later, but we'd still have them.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's keep our heads and look after our own. Young ones should still learn trades, because people will want someone they know doing their house for a while yet.
S3.think: It's still too soon: I'd get a few years as a proper builder but be watching the whole time. And I'd worry about having children into it, which we want after the wedding.
S3.do: Goes ahead with the wedding as planned, holds off buying a house for a couple of years and lives in the farm cottage while saving harder. Keeps working for her boss as long as there's work.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, but still able to sleep.
S3.quote: I don't think a robot gets asked in for tea.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets her keep the wedding but still delays the house. She places her hope in local trust and personal relationships, illustrated by Mrs Price. Decisions about children go through faith and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, with children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen, so there's no use panicking. I'd say keep working and keep your family close. Maybe by year eight I'd say something different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can mostly live my life as planned. Wedding, house, children, building with Mr Hughes and then Rhys when he takes over. I'd probably not think about it much until it was nearly here, which isn't clever, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house on the edge of town after the wedding, like we planned. I'd keep working and learning, and keep saving with Owen. I wouldn't go on any course or learn computers, I'd wait and see what the world looks like in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd be thinking about the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years you'd buy the house; with two you wouldn't. What makes the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and we'd have paid a good chunk off, and Owen's farm would have had time to sort itself out. Two years and we'd be stuck with a big loan and no work. It's not complicated, really, it's just how long you've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys. He's meant to take over the firm when Mr Hughes retires, and he'd be taking over something that might not last. I don't think anyone's told him to think about that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen, so there's no use panicking. Keep working and keep your family close.
S4.think: I can mostly live my life as planned: wedding, house, children, building with Mr Hughes and then Rhys. I'd probably not think about it much until it was nearly here, which isn't clever.
S4.do: Buys the house on the edge of town after the wedding as planned. Keeps working, learning and saving with Owen, and waits to see how things look in a few years rather than retraining.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly thinking about the wedding.
S4.quote: It's not complicated, really, it's just how long you've got.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her plans go ahead almost untouched, and she admits she'd put off thinking about it. Her house decision depends directly on the warning time. Her worry shifts to Rhys inheriting a firm that might not last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would land right on top of the wedding and the house and Owen's farm all at once. What would help is keeping work local, so firms like Mr Hughes's get the jobs instead of companies from miles away, and proper apprenticeships for whatever's left. Not handouts. I want to earn it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here would get through something like this because of chapel and family, not because of any government. That matters more than people in cities think.

headlineQuote: A lot of people round here would get through something like this because of chapel and family, not because of any government.
portrait: Elena Evans is a 27-year-old junior at a small family building firm in a market town, who struggles with measuring, avoids computers entirely and is saving with her fiancé Owen, a farmer's son, for a house and a chapel wedding next September. She's traditional and distrustful of new things that seem made for cities, and her worry in the milder pictures is mostly for her boss's family firm. The fast AGI picture alarms her because it would land on her wedding, house and Owen's farm at once, and she'd turn to family and chapel. With more warning her plans go ahead more and more as normal, and she admits she'd put off thinking about it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would land on her wedding, the house purchase and Owen's family farm all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping building work local for firms like her boss's, and proper apprenticeships for whatever work remains, rather than handouts.
